“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you take for him?”

“Sho, there’s ticks a plenty. I could have a thousand of ’em if I wanted to.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know mighty well you can’t. This is a pretty early tick, I reckon. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for him.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom got out a bit of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it wistfully. The temptation was very strong. At last he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the gap.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a trade.”

Tom put the tick in the percussion-cap box that had lately been the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom reached the little isolated frame schoolhouse, he strode in briskly, with the air of someone who had come with all honest speed. He hung his hat on a peg and flung himself into his seat with businesslike eagerness. The master, perched high in his great splint-bottom armchair, was dozing, lulled by the drowsy hum of study. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that when his name was said in full, it meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to hide behind a lie, when he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized with the electric sympathy of love; and that form was the only empty place on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He instantly said:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The master’s pulse seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The buzz of study died away. The pupils wondered if this reckless boy had lost his mind. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no mistaking the words.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astounding confession I have ever listened to. No mere ferule will answer for this offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm went to work until it was tired and the supply of switches had notably diminished. Then the order came:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

I beg you to say something for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to point out that, considering everything, he ought to be more open with me!”

I have never seen two men look at each other more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this speech. At first, I feared that Wemmick would be dismissed from his job at once. But that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, while Wemmick grew more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father, and you, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the greatest impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” Wemmick replied, growing bolder still. “I think you’re the other one.”

Once again they exchanged their strange looks, each apparently still unsure whether the other was making fun of him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it be so. Now, looking at you, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you were planning and arranging to have a pleasant home of your own one day, when you’ve grown tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams.’ You know more about such things than I do, since you have much fresher experience of them. But now, about this other matter. I’ll give you a case. Remember, I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I fully understood he was expressly admitting nothing.
